sections.title: Keys: Lesson 09, Regularization and model selection

keyTerms.definition: A lesson topic in CS229 covering techniques to constrain model complexity and improve generalization on new data.
The lesson subject about choosing among candidate models, a core part of the Regularization lesson.
Listed as instructors of the Stanford CS229 Machine Learning course for this lesson.
The ninth lesson in the course, focused on regularization and model selection.

recall.question: What is the topic of Lesson 09 in the Stanford CS229 course?
recall.answer: Lesson 09 covers Regularization and model selection. It is dated 2026-10-06 and taught by Tengyu Ma and Andrew Ng.

recall.question: Who teaches Lesson 09 of Stanford CS229?
recall.answer: The instructor listed for Lesson 09 is Tengyu Ma and Andrew Ng. The lesson is part of the Machine Learning (Stanford CS229) series.

keyTerms.definition: An objective function J_lambda(theta) equal to J(theta) plus lambda times a regularization term R(theta), with lambda >= 0.
The value of theta that maximizes the product of the likelihood over examples and the prior on theta.
A prior theta ~ N(0, tau^2 I) whose log equals -||theta||^2 / (2 tau^2), yielding the ridge penalty with lambda = 1/tau^2.
Any use of validation or test information during training or model selection, such as preprocessing or feature selection fit on all data.

recall.question: Why does l1 regularization tend to produce sparse solutions while l2 regularization usually does not?
recall.answer: The l1 ball has corners on the coordinate axes, so loss contours tend to meet it at corners, which are sparse. The l2 ball is smooth, so contact is almost never exactly sparse.

recall.question: How does k-fold cross-validation estimate validation performance?
recall.answer: Split the data into k folds. For each fold, train on the remaining k-1 folds and validate on the held-out fold, then average the k validation scores.

keyTerms.definition: A penalized regression that adds lambda times half the squared norm of theta to the loss, shrinking correlated weights rather than zeroing them.
An L1-penalized regression that picks one feature from a correlated group instead of sharing weight across them.
Choosing complexity by validation, k-fold CV, AIC, or train/validation/test splits to avoid overfitting.
A degree-8 polynomial with n = 12 where ridge at lambda = 1 lowers test MSE from about 2.4 to about 0.3.

recall.question: Why does ridge require a strictly positive lambda in its closed form or gradient descent implementation?
recall.answer: X^T X plus lambda I is positive definite only when lambda is greater than zero. A singularity complaint means lambda is not positive or there is a bug.

recall.question: Why is picking the model with the lowest training error not a valid model selection rule?
recall.answer: Training error always falls with complexity, so it always picks the most complex model and overfits. Validation error must guide the choice.

keyTerms.definition: A regularization coefficient that multiplies theta in the gradient, controlling weight decay strength in the update rule.
The regularization effect of shrinking parameters by factor one minus eta lambda at each gradient update step.
The sum of log likelihoods minus the squared norm of theta over two tau squared, plus a constant.
The negative log likelihood plus one over two tau squared times the squared norm of theta.

recall.question: What is the update rule for theta in exercise E09?
recall.answer: Theta updates as theta minus eta times the gradient of J lambda, which expands to one minus eta lambda times theta minus eta times the gradient of J.

recall.question: How does the log posterior relate to the ridge objective in exercise E10?
recall.answer: Maximizing the log posterior equals minimizing the negative log likelihood plus one over two tau squared times the squared norm of theta, where lambda equals one over tau squared.

keyTerms.definition: A failure where validation folds see test statistics through the mean and variance of the full dataset.
The process used on the full dataset that caused leakage during validation.
Held out data partitions that experienced optimistic error due to leakage.
The transformation component that must be fit inside each fold on training data only.

recall.question: What caused the optimistic validation error in E11?
recall.answer: Standardization used the full dataset, so validation folds saw test statistics through the mean and variance.

recall.question: How can the leakage problem be fixed?
recall.answer: Fit the scaler inside each fold on the training folds only.

keyTerms.definition: A team that uses nested cross validation to keep an untouched test set separate from model selection.
A team whose reported number is contaminated because the test set guided model choice.
A validation method that keeps a separate untouched test set apart from model selection.
Held out data used to evaluate a model, which Team A contaminated by letting it guide model choice.

recall.question: Why is Team A reported error optimistic by an unknown amount?
recall.answer: Team A used the test set to guide the choice of model, so the test set acted like a second validation set. This contamination means the reported error is optimistically biased by an unknown amount.

recall.question: What advantage does Team B nested CV approach provide?
recall.answer: Team B nested cross validation keeps an untouched test set that was never used during model selection, giving an unbiased evaluation.

keyTerms.definition: A least squares problem where the model has more parameters than data points, so many solutions fit the data exactly.
Among all parameter settings that fit the training data exactly, the one with the smallest overall size.

recall.question: According to the research question, how does GD compare to Adam with default settings on overparameterized least squares from small initialization?
recall.answer: The claim states that GD lands closer in l2 distance to the minimum-norm interpolator than Adam with default settings, on overparameterized least squares trained from small initialization.

keyTerms.definition: A curve in log lambda that decreases then increases, with a minimum at an interior point.
The logarithmic scale of the regularization parameter lambda used to plot the test-error curve.

recall.question: What shape does the test-error curve take in log lambda, and where is its minimum?
recall.answer: The test-error curve is U-shaped in log lambda, and its minimum occurs at an interior point.
